text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementAstronomyHere’s Why It’s So Hard to Boost a SatelliteNASA’s Swift telescope has burned up, months after a robot sent to save it failedWKBy Wanjiku Chebet Kanjumba11:00 AM CST on November 11, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleNASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory took its last look at the sky on Oct. 20, 2026, while orbiting about 171 miles (275 kilometers) above Earth. NASA ended the telescope’s mission three days later, because Swift had sunk so low that drag from the thin air there meant its telescopes couldn’t hold steady. The telescope reentered the atmosphere on Nov. 4 above the North Sumatra region of Indonesia and largely burned up, an abrupt ending to two decades spent observing powerful cosmic explosions.Powered By 1012.5K 00ShareNextStaySwift’s reentry comes after a failed rescue mission in the summer of 2026. LINK, a commercial robotic spacecraft sent to raise Swift into a safer orbit, reentered Earth’s atmosphere in September. The machine designed to save a falling satellite burned up first.As a Ph.D. candidate in aerospace engineering, I know that rescuing satellites is hard. I research how spacecraft approach and capture satellites, including objects that tumble uncontrollably.Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisement
